# Introduction

Picture a tea stall almost anywhere in India. A customer finishes a cup, points a phone at a printed QR code on the counter, and pays. Nobody asks for cash, and nobody asks for a card. In September 2026, UPI payments like this one happened about 80 crore times a day.

On 30 September 2026, Apple Pay arrived in India. It came about ten years after Apple's chief executive, Tim Cook, said during a visit to India in May 2016, "We want to bring Apple Pay to India."

But think about the customer at the tea stall. Their payment already works. It is quick, and the shopkeeper accepts it. So what can Apple offer someone who has no problem to solve? Why would anyone change a way of paying that already works?

# Two Ways to Pay

With Apple Pay, a customer adds a credit card to an iPhone or Apple Watch and then pays by holding the device near a card machine. At launch in India, it works only with Axis Bank credit cards on the Visa and Mastercard networks. Apple says the phone does not share the real card number with the shop. It uses a stand-in number instead, a method known as tokenisation, so the shop gets paid without seeing the card details.

UPI started as a way to move money directly from one bank account to another in real time, and today it can also be linked to RuPay credit cards. Any UPI app can pay any UPI QR code, whichever bank or app the shopkeeper uses. At launch, Apple Pay does not support UPI or RuPay cards.

So the two are not rival apps doing the same job. Apple Pay is a new way to use an existing credit card. To use it in India today, a person needs three things, an iPhone, an eligible Axis Bank credit card and a shop with a contactless card machine.

# Why the Tea Stall Has No Card Machine

Ask why the shopkeeper put up a QR code in the first place. Customers pay that way. Ask why customers pay that way, and the answer is that almost every shop has a QR code. Each new user makes UPI more useful for shops, and each new shop makes it more useful for users. Economists call this a network effect. Much of the system's value comes from the people already using it.

Payments have a special version of this problem. A payment system needs two groups at once, buyers and sellers, and each group mostly cares about how many of the other group have joined. This is called a two-sided market. Shops do not want to prepare for a method few customers use, and customers do not want a method few shops accept.

UPI got past that stage years ago. In 2021-22, it handled about 4,596 crore transactions. In 2025-26, it handled about 24,162 crore, more than five times as many. By June 2026, 55.49 crore users had registered on it. According to the Reserve Bank of India, UPI made up 85.5 percent of all digital payment transactions in India by number in the second half of 2025.

Changing a habit this widespread has a cost that is not paid in money. The customer has to learn a new routine, and the shopkeeper needs equipment that accepts it. This is a switching cost. Even card machines are being pulled toward UPI. In July 2026, the chief executive of Pine Labs, which supplies payment machines to shops, said that more than 70 percent of transactions on its in-store machines were already UPI.

# Apple's Shortcut, and Its Limit

Apple has one big advantage over a typical newcomer. It does not have to build a merchant network from nothing. Apple Pay runs on the Visa and Mastercard card networks, and Apple says it works anywhere that accepts contactless payments. At launch, it named merchants such as Zomato and Croma. In effect, Apple has borrowed one side of the two-sided market.

The customer side is harder. Today, only people who own an iPhone and hold an Axis Bank Visa or Mastercard credit card can use Apple Pay in India. So Apple can reach a large number of shops, but only a small number of customers.

For those who qualify, Apple Pay could offer reasons to choose it. Card users keep their card rewards, and online shoppers do not have to type card details. Giving people a reason to pick one product over another, other than price, is what economists call product differentiation. But these are possible reasons, not proof that people will switch. Apple Pay also does not need to replace UPI to be useful. The same person might scan a QR code for tea and tap a phone to buy a laptop.

# Final Thoughts

Back at the tea stall, nothing has changed. The customer still scans the code and walks away. Apple's challenge in India was never mainly about technology.

The real contest happens in the few seconds at the counter. A new way to pay has to change what someone does at that moment, and that moment is already filled by a habit millions of people repeat without thinking. Technology can be built or bought. A habit that already works can only be changed one person, and one payment, at a time.
